Driven: 2026 Subaru Trailseeker (e-Outback) Proves the Boxer Engine Isn't Everything
54 photos
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution
Same tune, different song. Known as the Trailseeker in the United States, the Subaru e-Outback is essentially the same electric SUV wearing a different nameplate for European customers. Both versions roll off the same assembly line at Subaru's Gunma Yajima plant in Japan, where production began in February 2026.
The e-Outback also shares its underpinnings with the Toyota bZ4X Touring , another product of the Japanese automakers' long-standing partnership. However, Subaru insists that its electric SUV has received its own engineering tweaks, including suspension tuning, intended to make it more off-road-ready than its Toyota-badged brother. The main question is: is there enough Subaru DNA beneath the skin to back up that claim?
At first glance, the e-Outback bears a clear family resemblance to its combustion-powered namesake. Its rugged proportions, raised stance, and generous plastic cladding suggest that Subaru hasn't forgotten what made the Outback popular in the first place. However, the electric version features a considerably smaller front grille, which makes sense considering that under the hood there is no internal combustion engine.
Above the headlights, the slim LED daytime running lights resemble Spock's raised eyebrows, a distinctive feature of Subaru's latest design language. It's a slightly unusual look, but one that gives the e-Outback, or the 2026 Trailseeker, a recognizable face.
Design evaluation Viewed from the side, the electric crossover looks more like a station wagon on stilts than a conventional SUV. In that respect, it follows the recipe established decades ago with the first-generation Legacy Outback, whose legacy lives on this battery-powered successor. The Forester, meanwhile, has taken the role of the more traditional SUV in Subaru's lineup, after the Tribeca's dismissal.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution The extensive plastic cladding around the wheel arches and lower body panels might initially seem excessive. However, I found myself appreciating those protective elements after an unscheduled encounter with some bushes during the off-road test. The paint emerged unscratched, and even the plastic showed no visible marks from the branches.
In other words, the crossover's rugged aspect isn't just for show. It's not dressed to impress, but to announce that it's ready for your next outdoor adventure.
Interior Assessment Step inside the Subaru e-Outback, and you'll discover an interior that gets quite a few things right, although some of the manufacturer's decisions might leave you scratching your head. For starters, there's no glovebox. Subaru needed that place for some technical components, so it left it without one of the most traditional storage compartments in a car ever.
However, it put a generous storage compartment between the front seats, with a clever dual-opening lid. Rather than being rear-hinged, it opens on either side, allowing both the driver and front passenger to access it comfortably. The compartment is wide but relatively shallow, yet there's more than enough room for your favorite road-trip snacks, with some space left over for essentials.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution There's no head-up display either, not even on the options list. Instead, Subaru placed the digital instrument panel high enough so you won't need an HUD. It's well organized, easy to read, and offers several customization options. You can't arrange everything everywhere, but there's enough flexibility to choose the information that matters most to you.
The center console features two wireless phone chargers, while the transmission controls, drive mode selectors, and camera buttons are positioned behind them, closer to the armrest. Below, the automaker added another open storage area, useful for a purse, some additional snacks, and a few USB charging ports.
Comfort equipment depends on the trim level, as usual. However, the good thing is that all versions are getting the same drivetrain. While the entry-level version comes with fabric upholstery, the top-shelf variant gets heated and cooled front seats, a panoramic glass roof that doesn't open, and a Harman Kardon premium audio system. For the U.S. market, the leather seats are one step above the Touring grade.
Those seated in the back have little to complain about. There's plenty of legroom and headroom. Three adults can sit comfortably. In addition, the seatback offers two reclining positions, allowing passengers to prioritize comfort or free up some additional cargo space, thanks to the 60/40 split-folding mechanism.
Driving take With two electric motors driving all four wheels, the 2026 Subaru Trailseeker (e-Outback) delivers its power smoothly and progressively, as you'd expect from an EV. However, stamp on the skinny pedal and the rear end squats slightly before the vehicle shoots forward like a cannonball. That's so Subaru.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution The automaker claims a 0 to 100 kph (0-62 mph) run in 4.4 seconds, making the e-Outback the quickest in the model in Subaru's current lineup by that measure. However, using a GPS-based smartphone app, we recorded times below four seconds with the battery charged above 80 percent. There was a catch, though. In our case, after two consecutive launches, the car became more relaxed, suggesting that its electronics were limiting performance to protect the powertrain.
Despite its impressive straight-line performance, the e-Outback isn't particularly interested in pretending to be a sports car. The steering feels somewhat numb, while the soft suspension allows noticeable body roll around corners. Interestingly, the vehicle maintains its composure and grips remarkably well, but the body movements discourage enthusiastic driving long before the chassis approaches its actual limits.
On the other hand, the same suspension setup makes the Trailseeker a remarkably smooth companion on uneven roads. Rather than chasing sharp handling, Subaru appears to prioritize ride quality and comfort, a decision that makes perfect sense considering the vehicle's intended purpose as a family car.
Fortunately, the braking system is more reassuring. The transition between the regenerative braking and conventional friction brakes is exceptionally smooth, with no perceptible change in pedal feel. In addition, the paddles behind the steering wheel let you adjust how aggressive the regenerative braking can be, although one-pedal-drive is not present.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution However, the biggest surprise comes when you leave the pavement behind. Despite riding on 20-inch wheels wrapped in Dunlop Sport Maxx tires, the e-Outback exceeded my expectations on a damp off-road course featuring steep climbs, descents, slide slopes, and plenty of mud.
Much of the credit goes to Subaru's X-MODE system, which manages traction and allows different degrees of wheelspin, depending on the selected setting. Whether climbing steep ramps covered in wet grass or negotiating muddy sections, the system continuously adjusted the available traction. I deliberately pushed the e-Outback into situations where grip was scarce, trying to find its limits. Yet, the electronics repeatedly stepped in to manage power delivery and save the day.
From behind the wheel, it's really tempting to believe that you're demonstrating some impressive off-road driving skills. In reality, electronics are doing much of the heavy lifting, helping you escape situations your own overconfidence might have gotten you into.
On one particular, grass-covered slope, the hill-descent function proved its ability to keep the car in a straight line. I didn't have to touch any pedals. No drama, no fuss, just the electronics quietly doing their job.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution The 8.5-inch ground clearance, short front overhang, and underbody protection further inspire confidence when tackling uneven terrain. Combined with the capable all-wheel-drive system, these features make the e-Outback (Trailseeker) a convincing choice for weekend adventurers, rather than another electric crossover that merely looks the part and struggles climbing a curb at the mall.
Everyday Living If the Outback's soft suspension and somewhat numb steering discourage spirited driving, they become welcome companions during the daily commute. The ride is great, the seats provide excellent support, and the cabin remains quiet, with little noticeable tire or wind noise. Generous side windows and the available panoramic glass roof, which has a retractable shade but cannot be opened, further enhance the sense of space.
Subaru also paid attention to some minor practical details. The doors extend over the lower sills, protecting them from mud and road grime. After our off-road adventure, I was particularly grateful for this arrangement. Otherwise, I might still be cleaning mud off my pants, shoes, and upholstery. It's not a first in the industry, but there are many other SUV-manufacturers that don't make this.
The cargo area is spacious and regularly shaped, although the loading lip is higher than on a conventional station wagon. Considering the vehicle's generous ground clearance, that's a reasonable compromise. Besides, taller drivers might appreciate not having to bend quite so far when retrieving luggage.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution For the onboard infotainment system, the car proved effective. It seamlessly paired wirelessly with Android Auto and Apple CarPlay devices, while the built-in navigation system offers another useful feature. Enter a charging station as your destination, and the vehicle automatically starts battery preconditioning to prepare it for DC charging. Ideally, the station should be at least 30 minutes away, depending on the outside temperature.
During our test, we observed a charging power of 113 kW just a few minutes after plugging in, with an estimated time of approximately 30 minutes to reach 80 percent. When we returned 40 minutes later, the battery was sitting comfortably at the 80% charging limit, for another adventure. We had deliberately selected that limit to help preserve battery longevity.
Energy consumption ranged between 20 and 24 kWh/100 km (2.6-3.1 miles/kWh), depending on the driving conditions and how enthusiastically we used the accelerator. With the battery at 80 percent, the instrument cluster estimated about 170 miles (274 km) of remaining range, suggesting a real-world range of about 200 miles (320 km) on a full charge. Considering that ambient temperatures ranged between 39 and 63 degrees Fahrenheit (4-17 Celsius), that's a respectable result for an all-wheel-drive electric SUV riding on 20-inch wheels.
The 20-inch wheels fitted on our test vehicle also come with an efficiency penalty compared with the available 18-inch alternatives. If maximizing range is your priority, the smaller ones would be the better choice.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution Subaru could probably have squeezed a few more miles out of the 74.2 kWh battery with a more aerodynamically optimized body. Instead, it chose to build something that actually looks like a Subaru, rather than another anonYmous electric crossover shaped primarily by the demands of the wind tunnel and the accountants.
Test Drive Round-up There's plenty of Subaru DNA included in the e-Outback, or the Trailseeker, bodywork, and I'm not talking about its vivid blue paint. The way it reminded me of a second-generation Forester, particularly when the pavement disappeared and the going got tough. There's no flat-four engine under the hood, no conventional driveshaft connecting the axles, and no mechanical center differential distributing torque.
Yet, the way the electric all-wheel-drive system manages traction feels remarkably familiar to anyone who has spent time behind the wheel of a traditional Subaru.
The e-Outback does everything you'd expect from an adventurous crossover, and then some. It also proves that electrification doesn't necessarily mean abandoning the qualities that made a brand successful in the first place.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution There's even a little luxury for those who enjoy getting away from civilization without giving up every creature comfort. With the available vehicle-to-load capability, you could take an espresso machine into the wilderness and enjoy a proper morning coffee surrounded by nature. Just remember to plan your charging stops and keep an eye on the remaining range.
As for the pricing, we're using the American Trailseeker as our reference, since it's the U.S.-market counterpart of the e-Outback tested here. The Trailseeker starts at $39,995 for the Premium. The Limited starts at $43,995 and ads a 120-volt power outlet in the cargo area, while the better-equipped Touring costs $46,555. The Touring Leather ads another $300.
These are manufacturer-suggested retail prices , excluding destination charges, sales taxes, and registration fees. Our e-Outback tested was about the same price as its American sibling, at roughly EUR 50,000.
Yes, we know there are many other electric SUVs on the market that are worth considering. Some of them may offer better efficiency or sharper handling. But if you're looking for the same peace of mind you've come to expect from Subaru, or from a dependable Toyota, there's little reason to change a winning recipe simply because automotive fashion has moved on.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution
The e-Outback, like its Trailseeker twin brother, isn't perfect. Its steering could use more feedback, its energy consumption is not the best in class, and the missing glovebox remains a peculiar decision. But it's comfortable, generously equipped, surprisingly capable off-road, and unmistakably Subaru where it matters most.
The boxer engine may be gone, but the adventurous spirit is alive and kickin'.
Pros
Great off-road abilities
Sportscar-like acceleration
Roomy cabin for six-feet passengers
Cons
Numb steering
Unimpressive energy efficiency
No glovebox
